title: Monadic logic: unary predicates and finite models

based_on.title: Computational perspectives on the classical decision problem, Lecture 2: The monadic fragment
based_on.pages: Logical slides 3–7 (expanded PDF pages 27–71); positive-domain bound corrected

summary: Unary predicates cannot distinguish enough copies of the same profile: capped representatives give finite models and a terminating decision procedure.
abstract: Can a first-order sentence require infinitely many objects when its only relations describe one object at a time? With finitely many unary predicates, equality, and no constants or functions, the answer is no, even when universal and existential quantifiers alternate. Each object has a finite list of predicate truth values. A sentence can count objects with the same list only as far as its quantifiers allow, so retaining a bounded number of representatives of each list preserves its truth. We prove this by tracking which assigned objects are equal and which predicates they satisfy, and then turn the resulting finite model bound into an explicit search through finite truth tables. Examples explain why equality needs several representatives and why a binary relation changes the situation.
